query: For high-entropy-alloy bond coats used in thermal barrier coating systems for high-temperature applications, what single intervention could improve coating durability and reliability? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should remain effective, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of an oxidation‐resistant element (via Y2O3 nanoparticle incorporation) to CrMnFeCoNi HEA bond coats will promote the in situ formation of a continuous, protective oxide scale that limits Mn depletion and improves oxidation resistance at high temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy bond coat exhibiting non-protective oxidation with Mn depletion during high-temperature exposure in air.
generation.intervention: Incorporation of approximately 1 wt% Y2O3 nanoparticles into the HEA bond coat during fabrication.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation in air (e.g., 950–1100 °C) where the formation of protective oxide layers is critical, and where the alloy is normally exposed to aggressive oxidation conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, adherent protective oxide scale (likely a Y-stabilized Cr2O3-based or equivalent oxide) that inhibits outward Mn diffusion.
generation.mechanism: Y2O3 acts as an oxidation-resistant additive by scavenging oxygen and promoting the nucleation and growth of a compact and stable oxide barrier. This barrier limits the outward diffusion of Mn, thereby maintaining the alloy's bulk composition and enhancing mechanical and oxidation resistance compared to the untreated state.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated baseline, the Y2O3-modified HEA bond coat will show a reduced oxidation rate, minimized Mn depletion, and improved high-temperature durability and reliability.
generation.baseline: Unmodified CrMnFeCoNi HEA bond coats where high-temperature air exposure leads to non-protective Mn oxide formation and consequential alloy degradation.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected to be effective primarily under high-temperature air conditions typical of thermal barrier coating applications (∼950–1100 °C) and may not extend to environments with extreme oxygen partial pressures or temperatures significantly different from the test range.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of the durability improvement may be sensitive to the exact amount, distribution, and processing of Y2O3, and additional kinetic effects during oxidation may introduce variability. Further detailed studies will be required to optimize the additive level and verify the protective scale formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA bond coat samples: one set with 1 wt% Y2O3 addition and one untreated baseline. Expose both sets to high-temperature oxidation in air (e.g., hold at 950–1100 °C for a fixed duration) under identical conditions. Use in situ X-ray diffraction (HTXRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to monitor oxide scale formation, phase evolution, and microstructural changes. Additionally, perform elemental profiling (e.g., EDS) to track Mn depletion across the oxide scale and the underlying substrate.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and uniformity (via SEM)
Phase composition of the oxide layer (via HTXRD)
Mn concentration profiles (via EDS or similar techniques)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y2O3-modified samples do not develop a continuous, compact protective oxide scale (or show similar non-protective oxide formation as the baseline), and if oxidation kinetics and Mn depletion rates are not significantly improved relative to the untreated samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In alloys for high-temperature applications, at least one protective oxide among BeO, Cr2O3, Al2O3, and SiO2 are desirable to form, and that is why most of the alloys for high-temperature applications add these elements to form an oxide barrier for better oxidation resistance []. Previous studies have indicated that Cr2O3 is the sole stable phase in the Cr-O system, known for its compact structure and superior oxidation resistance []. However, it is noteworthy that Cr2O3 was not detected in the in situ XRD analysis conducted for this study. It can be reasonably inferred that non-existence of a Cr2O3 layer caused further outward diffusion of Mn, leading to the formation of Mn3O4, as can be seen from the XRD scan at a temperature of 950 °C.

Moreover, the addition of Y2O3 forms oxide-dispersion-strengthened (ODS) alloys, which exhibit exceptional performance []. ODS alloys maintain excellent high-temperature strength and oxidation resistance even at temperatures above 1000 °C, making them suitable for advanced applications such as aerospace engines, gas turbines, and other high-temperature oxidation-resistant components. Debta et al. [] concluded that Y2O3 can refine the microstructure of coatings, enhance their fracture toughness and ductility, and reduce their wear rate. Fu et al. [] discovered that when laser cladding iron-based alloy powders containing different amounts of La2O3 on rail materials, the addition of La2O3 decreased the width of the interface fusion zone, reduced the number of columnar crystals in the coating, and refined the grains. Cui et al. [] successfully prepared FeCoNiCrMo HEA coatings and CeO2/FeCoNiCrMo composite coatings on the surface of TC4 alloy using laser cladding technology. The results showed that the addition of CeO2 powder reduced the crack sensitivity of the HEA coating, refined the grains, and improved the coating’s strength and toughness.

chosen.approach: Oxidation‐resistant element addition to form protective oxide scale
